claims.text: Selective dealloying of a prealloyed noble metal–based high-entropy alloy can produce a three-dimensional nanoporous framework.
The resulting nanoporous framework can retain a high-entropy composition.
The resulting framework can exhibit enhanced catalytic properties.
The precursor is a homogeneous alloy containing uniformly distributed catalytically active noble metals and more reactive, less noble metals.
Electrochemical dealloying can preferentially remove less noble metal atoms from the alloy.
Controlled potential or current density and etching time can enable selective dissolution without structural collapse.
The proposed dealloying process can be operated at room temperature.
Dealloying produces a porous, interconnected network with nanometer-scale ligaments and pores.
Selective dissolution of less noble metals leaves a framework composed of the remaining noble metals.
The framework left by selective dissolution has high surface area.
High-entropy character stabilizes a heterogeneous elemental distribution and complex surface structure.
The complex, high-surface-area structure can increase the density of catalytic active sites.
An increased density of active sites can enhance catalytic activity.
The dealloyed nanoframework will have significantly greater surface area than a fully dense noble metal–based high-entropy alloy.
The dealloyed nanoframework will show improved catalytic performance, such as lower overpotential and higher current density, relative to a fully dense alloy.
A conventionally fabricated bulk noble metal–based high-entropy alloy has lower catalytic efficiency because its exposed surface area is limited.
The success of dealloying is sensitive to alloy composition and processing parameters.
Overly aggressive etching may cause ligament coarsening or structural collapse.
Insufficient process control may fail to produce the desired porous structure.
